summary: This memo discusses inter-domain policy routing, covering an overview of its functions and a discussion of experiments, in support of advancing it. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Different networks have different rules about which roads they will let your traffic use. This paper explains a system that takes those rules into account.

questions: how does inter-domain policy routing work
subtitle: Policy-based routing that respects administrative domain rules

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew to thousands of networks in the early 1990s, existing routing protocols could not choose paths that satisfy both user service needs (like delay or reliability) and domain policies (what traffic a domain would carry).
tldr.mechanism: IDPR (Inter-Domain Policy Routing) lets source domains specify routes across administrative domains, with policy gateways checking that each path respects the rules of every domain it transits. Route servers compute paths from domain-level topology and policy information.
tldr.outcome: The system was prototyped and deployed experimentally, and IDPR was integrated into the gated routing software. However, it required widespread deployment to be useful, and never achieved critical mass as BGP and other simpler protocols became dominant.

today: RFC 1477 is informational. IDPR has not become a standard protocol. While the IDPR architecture and protocols (RFC 1478, 1479) were fully specified and implementations exist, simpler routing approaches became dominant in the Internet, and IDPR remains in the historical record as an experimental system.

sections.title: Inter-Domain Routing with Policies
sections.content:
RFC 1477 describes the motivation and design overview of IDPR (Inter-Domain Policy Routing). IDPR is an approach to routing at the inter-domain level that respects not only connectivity but also the policies of each administrative domain. An administrative domain (AD) is a collection of networks and routers governed by a single organization—a company, ISP, or university network.

As the Internet grew in the late 1980s and early 1990s, domain administrators increasingly had business, political, or technical reasons to restrict what traffic they would carry. IDPR was designed to let the source domain (the one generating traffic) specify routes that satisfy its service requirements while honoring the restrictions of every transit domain along the path. Without IDPR, traffic might be routed through domains that block it or provide poor service.
sections.eli5: When you send data across the Internet, it goes through many different networks, each with its own rules. IDPR finds a path that follows all the rules.

sections.title: System Architecture and Components
sections.content:
IDPR comprises several kinds of entities. Policy gateways are routers at domain boundaries that forward data along policy routes and participate in path setup. Path agents run inside policy gateways and act on behalf of hosts, selecting routes and managing paths. Route servers compute policy routes from domain topology and policy information, working with source policy requirements provided by path agents. Mapping servers resolve host addresses to administrative domains. Configuration servers store policy information for domains.

Each domain advertises its transit policies (what services it offers and what restrictions apply) and receives source policies (what services traffic sources need). Route servers use link-state routing information distribution—every domain's representative sends its routing information to every other domain. When source and destination are known, the route server generates a policy route: a sequence of domains, each of which offers the required services and obeys domain restrictions.
sections.eli5: Some computers (gateways) live at the edges of networks. They ask a route server "find me a path that obeys all the rules." The route server checks all the networks and says "go through network A, then B, then C."

sections.title: Policies, Route Selection, and Forwarding
sections.content:
Administrators define two kinds of policies. Transit policies specify what the domain offers: access restrictions (some traffic barred), quality of service (delay, throughput, reliability), and cost (charged per byte or session). Source policies specify what traffic originating in the domain needs: which domains to favor or avoid, acceptable quality of service, and acceptable cost.

IDPR uses two main message types: data messages (user traffic) and control messages (policy and routing information). Data messages travel using source routing: the path is specified by the source, giving sources complete control over traffic. IDPR encapsulates messages at domain boundaries so they appear as normal packets to intra-domain routing, preserving backward compatibility. IDPR is invisible to domains and hosts that do not implement it; they treat IDPR traffic like any other.
sections.eli5: Before sending data, the source asks "what do you offer?" Each network replies with its rules: "we're fast but expensive," or "we're free but slow." The source picks a path that matches what it needs.

sections.title: Security, Scalability, and Experimental Status
sections.content:
IDPR messages carry integrity and authenticity values computed using digital signatures (RSA applied to message hashes) or other algorithms specified by the IANA, so receiving domains can verify that control messages are genuine and have not been tampered with. Timestamps help reject stale messages. Control messages must carry valid signatures; data messages are left to higher layers for integrity checking.

The RFC describes two implementations: an IDPR prototype built in 1990–1991 by USC, SAIC, and BBN on Sun workstations, and the integration into gated, a widely-used Unix routing daemon. Experiments with the prototype successfully demonstrated path setup, adaptation to component failures, and reconfiguration to policy changes. However, IDPR required widespread deployment to be useful, and in practice, simpler approaches like BGP eventually dominated inter-domain routing. The gated version remains available, but IDPR has remained largely experimental and informational.
sections.eli5: IDPR signs its control messages so no one can forge them. The system was tested in laboratories and added to real routing software, but it never became the standard way of routing because people liked simpler approaches better.
